definition: Prescient means showing knowledge of events before they happen; able to foresee what is coming.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word prescient. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know prescient should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her 2005 essay warning that phones would reshape childhood now looks remarkably prescient.
Farsighted means planning sensibly for the future; prescient is stronger, suggesting someone seemed to actually know what was coming.
Prophetic goes beyond prescient — it implies foretelling the future with almost supernatural, oracle-like accuracy.

A visionary imagines bold possible futures and works to bring them about — visionary founders, visionary architects. The claim is about imagination and ambition. Prescient is a verdict passed in hindsight: events proved the person right. A visionary dreams what could come; a prescient person turns out to have known what did.

Clairvoyant claims an outright supernatural power to see what cannot be seen — the word of psychics and crystal balls. Prescient stays inside the natural world: it credits insight so sharp that someone seemed to know what was coming, and we usually award it after events prove them right.

Shrewd means sharp and practical about the situation in front of you — a shrewd negotiator reads the room, the market, the moment. It is sharpness about the present. Prescient reaches past the present entirely: it credits someone with apparent knowledge of events that had not yet happened.

Prescient means showing knowledge of events before they happen; able to foresee what is coming.
The city planner's prescient decision to reserve land for flood channels seemed wasteful at the time, but it spared thousands of homes when the record storms finally came.
The planner acted as if she already knew the floods were coming, and events proved her right — accurately foreseeing the future is exactly what prescient describes.
Prescient is usually a compliment paid in hindsight: we call a warning, essay, or decision prescient only after events prove it right.
Common collocations: 'remarkably prescient,' 'a prescient warning,' 'proved prescient.'

In 1998, the head librarian began photographing the county's oldest land deeds, a project the board tolerated as a harmless hobby.
She argued that a single disaster could erase two centuries of records, and she spent her lunch hours working through the vault, drawer by drawer.
When the river rose in 2011 and took the archive's basement with it, hers were the only copies in existence.
The same trustees who had once trimmed her budget now called the project prescient.
She always corrected them gently: she had not known the flood was coming, she said, only that something someday would.
